unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ironhart Steel Co is a steel rolling mill in Country X, operating for 9 years with 85 employees. It makes reinforcing bar for construction firms, with annual revenue of $9.6 million. The government imposed an import quota capping foreign steel bar at 40,000 tonnes a year, down from 95,000 tonnes, to protect domestic mills. Ironhart's output rose 12% in the first six months and it hired 14 workers.

The ministry is now consulting on whether to tighten the quota further to 25,000 tonnes or relax it to 60,000 tonnes. Construction firms argue imported steel keeps building costs down and want the relaxed limit. Ironhart wants the tighter quota kept. The managing director must decide whether to lobby for the tighter quota or invest $1.2 million in a new rolling line to stay competitive.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: An import quota is a physical limit set by a government on the quantity of a good that can be imported into a country over a given period [2].

knowledge_max_2: physical limit set by a government on imports
limits the quantity over a given period / protects domestic producers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ironhart Steel Co of the import quota on foreign steel bar.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The quota restricts foreign competition [k], so construction firms buy more domestic steel and Ironhart's output rose 12% in the first six months [app]. Benefit 2: Higher and more stable demand [k] let the mill hire 14 new workers and keep revenue of $9.6 million flowing [app].

knowledge_max_2: reduces foreign competition / protects domestic producers
raises demand, sales and revenue
application_max_2: output rose 12% in the first six months
hired 14 new workers / $9.6 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the import quota for construction firms in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The quota caps foreign steel bar at 40,000 tonnes a year, down from 95,000 tonnes [k], so builders face shortages of cheaper imported steel [app] and must pay more for domestic steel, raising building costs [an]. Disadvantage 2: With less foreign competition [k], domestic mills can keep reinforcing bar prices high [app], squeezing construction firms' profit margins on fixed-price contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: limits supply of imported steel / causes shortages
domestic prices stay high with less competition
application_max_2: 40,000 tonnes cap / down from 95,000 tonnes
cheaper imported steel unavailable / builders must use domestic steel
analysis_max_2: raises building costs for construction firms
squeezes profit margins on fixed-price contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironhart Steel Co should lobby the ministry to keep the tighter 25,000-tonne quota, or invest $1.2 million in a new rolling line to stay competitive? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lobbying for the tighter 25,000-tonne quota shields Ironhart from foreign competition [k], which already lifted its output by 12% and supports revenue of $9.6 million [app], protecting the 14 jobs created [an]. However, protection depends on the ministry's final decision [k]; if imports are relaxed to 60,000 tonnes, the mill loses that advantage [app], squeezing profit and putting those jobs at risk [an]. A $1.2 million rolling line would make the business more efficient whether or not the quota is tightened. Overall, Ironhart should invest in the rolling line because being cost-competitive is safer than relying on government protection [eval], although lobbying for the tighter quota remains sensible as a short-term back-up while output is rising [eval].

knowledge_max_2: protection shields domestic producers from foreign competition
protection depends on government decisions / is risky to rely on
application_max_2: output rose 12% / 14 jobs / $9.6 million revenue
25,000 tonnes vs 60,000 tonnes consultation
analysis_max_2: protects jobs and revenue in the short term
risk to sales and profit if the quota is relaxed
evaluation_max_2: weighs lobbying for protection against investing in competitiveness; justified recommendation with figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
CaneValley Foods Ltd is a manufacturer of sauces and jams in Country X, operating for 7 years with 120 employees. It imports 3,000 tonnes of cane sugar a year at $480 per tonne. The government introduced an import quota of 1,800 tonnes a year plus a 20% tariff on sugar above the quota, so the extra 1,200 tonnes now cost $576 per tonne, adding $115,200 a year to costs.

The managing director can switch the shortfall to domestic beet sugar at $545 per tonne, adding $78,000 a year to costs, or lobby the ministry to raise the quota. Lobbying could take 18 months with no guarantee of success. The beet sugar supply is reliable. The board must decide which option best protects profit margins.

questions.question_text: Define 'import licence'.
questions.model_answer: An import licence is a permit issued by a government allowing a business to import certain goods, used to control the quantity or value of imports [2].

knowledge_max_2: a permit issued by a government
allows certain goods to be imported / used to control import quantity or value

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why CaneValley Foods might lobby the ministry to raise the sugar quota instead of switching to domestic beet sugar.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Switching to beet sugar at $545 per tonne adds $78,000 a year to costs [k], which successful lobbying would avoid by restoring more cane sugar imports beyond the 1,800-tonne quota [app]. Reason 2: Successful lobbying would let the business buy all 3,000 tonnes at $480 per tonne [k], avoiding the $115,200 a year tariff paid on the 1,200-tonne shortfall [app].

knowledge_max_2: switching to beet sugar raises costs
a larger quota restores cheaper imported supply
application_max_2: $545 per tonne / $78,000 a year extra cost
3,000 tonnes at $480 / $115,200 a year tariff on the 1,200-tonne shortfall

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the sugar import quota creates for CaneValley Foods.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The 1,800-tonne quota forces the business to pay a 20% tariff on the extra 1,200 tonnes at $576 per tonne [k], adding $115,200 a year to costs [app] and squeezing profit margins on its sauces and jams [an]. Problem 2: Cane sugar supply is capped [k], so CaneValley may not secure its full 3,000-tonne yearly need [app], risking production delays and lost sales to retail buyers [an].

knowledge_max_2: quota restricts import quantity / forces tariff on the overflow
capped supply may disrupt production
application_max_2: $576 per tonne / 1,200 tonnes above the quota / 20% tariff
3,000-tonne yearly need / $115,200 a year added cost
analysis_max_2: squeezes profit margins on sauces and jams
production delays / lost sales to retail buyers

questions.question_text: Do you think CaneValley Foods should switch to domestic beet sugar or lobby the ministry for a larger quota? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching to beet sugar guarantees a reliable supply [k]; at $545 per tonne the 1,200-tonne shortfall adds $78,000 a year, less than the $115,200 tariff bill on imported sugar above the quota [app], so margins are protected immediately [an]. Lobbying could restore the full 3,000 tonnes at $480 per tonne [k], saving $115,200 a year if successful [app], but it may take 18 months with no guarantee of success [an]. Overall, CaneValley should switch to beet sugar now because $78,000 a year is cheaper than the tariff and secures supply straight away [eval], even though lobbying is worth pursuing as a longer-term aim in parallel [eval].

knowledge_max_2: switching to beet sugar secures supply
lobbying could restore cheaper full imports
application_max_2: $545 per tonne / $78,000 a year vs $115,200 tariff bill
3,000 tonnes at $480 / 18 months to lobby
analysis_max_2: margins protected immediately by switching
lobby success uncertain and slow
evaluation_max_2: weighs switching now against lobbying for a larger quota; justified recommendation with figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Rosewood Fashion is a clothing retailer in Country X with 14 stores and 230 employees. It imports 70% of its $4.8 million stock (about $3.36 million) from outside the Aster Trade Bloc and pays an 18% import tariff on this clothing. Rosewood sells mostly to middle-income families through high-street stores. Country X joins the Aster Trade Bloc on 1 January, removing the tariff on clothing from the other 6 member countries.

Two bloc-based suppliers have offered to supply Rosewood at prices 15% below its current non-bloc supplier, a saving of about $504,000 a year. Its current supplier, which is outside the bloc, has worked with Rosewood for 8 years and gives 60 days' credit. The managing director must decide whether to switch suppliers.

questions.question_text: Define 'member state'.
questions.model_answer: A member state is a country that has joined a trade bloc and agreed to follow its rules, such as trading without tariffs with other member countries [2].

knowledge_max_2: a country that has joined a trade bloc
agreed to follow the bloc's rules / trades on agreed terms with other members

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Rosewood Fashion of Country X joining the Aster Trade Bloc.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The 18% import tariff on clothing from the other 6 member countries is removed [k], so the imported garments that make up 70% of its $4.8 million stock become cheaper to buy [app]. Advantage 2: Bloc-based suppliers offered prices 15% below its current supplier [k], saving about $504,000 a year on the $3.36 million of imported garments [app].

knowledge_max_2: tariff removal lowers import costs
cheaper bloc-based suppliers
application_max_2: 18% tariff / 6 member countries / 70% of $4.8 million stock
$504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Rosewood Fashion could face if it switches to these bloc-based suppliers.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Its current supplier gives 60 days' credit [k]; new bloc suppliers may demand payment on order, straining cash flow [app] across 14 stores stocking seasonal lines [an]. Problem 2: Switching after 8 years means unproven quality and reliability [k]; faulty garments would damage Rosewood's brand image [app], leading to lost customers and lower repeat sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: new suppliers may end 60 days' credit terms
switching risks unproven quality and reliability
application_max_2: 60 days' credit / 14 stores stocking seasonal lines
8 years with the current supplier / Rosewood's brand image
analysis_max_2: cash-flow strain across the stores
brand damage / lost customers and lower repeat sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Rosewood Fashion should switch to the bloc-based suppliers when Country X joins the Aster Trade Bloc, or keep its existing supplier? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Switching removes the 18% tariff and saves about $504,000 a year on $3.36 million of imports [k], lifting profit across its 14 stores [app] without raising prices for middle-income families [an]. However, keeping the current supplier preserves 60 days' credit and 8 years of trust [k]; unknown suppliers risk quality and cash-flow problems [app], which could hurt the brand more than the saving is worth [an]. Overall, Rosewood should switch to the bloc-based suppliers because $504,000 a year is a major saving and bloc membership gives lasting tariff-free access [eval], although it should negotiate credit terms close to the existing 60 days before committing [eval].

knowledge_max_2: switching cuts import costs / tariff removed
keeping the supplier preserves credit and trust
application_max_2: $504,000 a year saving on $3.36 million of imports / 14 stores
60 days' credit / 8 years with current supplier / 18% tariff
analysis_max_2: higher profit without raising prices
risk to brand and cash flow from unknown suppliers
evaluation_max_2: weighs switching for the saving against keeping the trusted supplier; justified recommendation with figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Kibale Tea Co runs 3 tea estates in Country X and has operated for 11 years with 95 employees. It exports 60% of its output in 20 kg sacks through brokers. Kibale is a member of the Tzara Free Trade Area, where member countries do not charge tariffs on goods traded between members, though each member sets its own tariff on tea from outside the area.

The managing director has identified a new buyer market in another member country where demand for premium loose-leaf tea is growing at 9% a year. Entering it would cost $300,000 for distribution and marketing, with projected first-year sales of $750,000. Alternatively, Kibale could focus on existing non-member markets, where demand is flat but no marketing spend is needed.

questions.model_answer: A free trade area is a group of countries that agree to trade goods between themselves without tariffs, while each member keeps its own tariff on goods imported from outside the area [2].

knowledge_max_2: a group of countries trading goods without tariffs between members
each member keeps its own tariff on goods from outside the area

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Kibale Tea Co might enter the new member market.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Tea exported to another Tzara Free Trade Area member country faces no tariff [k], unlike sales to non-member countries [app]. Reason 2: Demand for premium loose-leaf tea in the new market is growing at 9% a year [k], with projected first-year sales of $750,000 against a $300,000 entry cost [app].

rising demand in the new market

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $300,000 launch cost must be paid before sales arrive [k], straining cash flow in a business that earns most revenue from its 60% export share [app], delaying other investments [an]. Problem 2: Established member-country tea growers already know their home market [k], so Kibale may have to cut prices or spend heavily on promotion [app], reducing profit per kg on its premium teas [an].

questions.model_answer: Entering the new member market gives tariff-free access and demand growing at 9% a year [k], with projected first-year sales of $750,000, far above the $300,000 entry cost [app], so the investment could be recovered within the first year [an]. However, non-member markets need no entry spend [k]; demand is flat rather than falling, so focusing there protects cash flow [app], although the business misses a growing tariff-free market and long-term revenue [an]. Overall, Kibale should enter the member market because tariff-free trading and 9% annual demand growth make $300,000 a sound investment [eval], provided management tracks the $750,000 sales forecast against actual results [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Copperton Appliances Ltd manufactures washing machines in Country X, operating for 13 years with 260 employees. Annual revenue is $14 million, of which $4.9 million comes from customers in the Meridian Trade Bloc, where its machines are sold through 9 electrical retailers. On 1 March the bloc raised its common external tariff on washing machines from 10% to 28%, adding about $85 to the landed cost of each machine.

Copperton could build an assembly plant inside the bloc for $2.5 million, employing 60 workers and making bloc sales tariff-free. Alternatively, it could keep production in Country X and raise bloc prices by 10%, though its bloc dealers warn sales could fall by 15%. The board must decide which option protects its bloc revenue.

questions.question_text: Define 'customs union'.
questions.model_answer: A customs union is a trade bloc in which member countries remove tariffs on trade between themselves and agree a common external tariff on goods coming from outside the bloc [2].

knowledge_max_2: member countries remove tariffs between themselves
members agree a common external tariff on goods from outside the bloc

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Copperton Appliances might build an assembly plant inside the Meridian Trade Bloc.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Bloc sales of $4.9 million a year would avoid the common external tariff after it rose from 10% to 28% [k], keeping its washing machines competitively priced [app]. Reason 2: A plant inside the bloc keeps tariff-free access permanently [k], securing bloc revenue of $4.9 million a year even if the tariff rises again [app].

knowledge_max_2: avoids the higher common external tariff
secures permanent tariff-free access / keeps prices competitive
application_max_2: $4.9 million bloc revenue / sold through 9 electrical retailers
tariff rose from 10% to 28% / about $85 added per machine

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Copperton Appliances could face if it builds the assembly plant inside the bloc.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $2.5 million build cost is a large upfront outlay [k], which drains liquidity for a business with $14 million revenue [app], increasing financial risk if bloc sales disappoint [an]. Problem 2: Running an overseas site adds management complexity [k]; coordinating 60 new workers and shipping parts across the border [app] stretches existing management and may slow decisions [an].

knowledge_max_2: large upfront investment / cash-flow strain
extra management complexity abroad
application_max_2: $2.5 million build cost / $14 million revenue
60 new workers / shipping parts across the border
analysis_max_2: financial risk if bloc sales disappoint
stretched management / slower decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperton Appliances should build the assembly plant inside the bloc, or keep production in Country X and raise bloc prices? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the plant protects $4.9 million of annual bloc revenue [k]; avoiding the 28% tariff that adds $85 per machine keeps Copperton competitive [app], letting steady sales repay the $2.5 million cost [an]. However, staying in Country X avoids that outlay and keeps $14 million revenue undisturbed [k]; a 10% price rise risks losing 15% of bloc sales, about $320,000 of revenue [app], but keeps production simple and local [an]. Overall, Copperton should build the plant, because tariff-free access secures the bloc market for the long term, whereas paying 28% or raising prices erodes bloc demand [eval], even though the $2.5 million cost must be carefully financed [eval].

knowledge_max_2: building inside the bloc avoids the common external tariff
staying avoids the large upfront outlay / keeps production simple
application_max_2: $4.9 million bloc revenue / $85 added per machine / $2.5 million plant
10% price rise risks 15% sales fall / $14 million revenue
analysis_max_2: steady sales repay the plant cost / long-term security
higher prices erode bloc demand / about $320,000 revenue risk
evaluation_max_2: weighs building inside the bloc against staying in Country X and raising prices; justified recommendation with figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Vireo Bicycles Ltd is a bicycle manufacturer in Country X, operating for 8 years with 140 employees. Country X has voted to leave the Aster Trade Bloc, a single market, after 12 years as a member. About 55% of Vireo's output is exported to bloc countries, generating $8 million a year. Under the exit deal, exports to the bloc face a new 8% tariff from January instead of zero tariff.

Vireo estimates the tariff would add $640,000 a year to its bloc costs. The managing director has identified a business park in a bloc member country where a final-assembly facility could be built for $1.8 million, employing 50 workers, restoring tariff-free access. Bloc demand for bicycles is growing at 6% a year. The board must decide whether to invest.

questions.question_text: Define 'single market'.
questions.model_answer: A single market is a trade bloc in which goods, services, workers and capital can move freely between member countries as if they were one internal market [2].

knowledge_max_2: trade bloc with free movement of goods, services, workers and capital
members act as one internal market / no internal tariffs

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Vireo Bicycles might build the final-assembly facility inside the bloc.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Assembly inside a member country keeps bloc exports tariff-free [k], avoiding the new 8% tariff on $8 million of exports, worth $640,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Bloc demand for bicycles is growing at 6% a year [k], so a tariff-free facility lets Vireo capture that growth with 50 local workers [app].

knowledge_max_2: keeps exports tariff-free / avoids the new tariff
captures growing bloc demand
application_max_2: 8% tariff on $8 million of exports / $640,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Vireo Bicycles of the new 8% tariff if it stays in Country X.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Exports to bloc countries worth $8 million a year face the 8% tariff [k], adding $640,000 a year to costs [app] and squeezing profit margins on 55% of its output [an]. Disadvantage 2: Vireo must absorb the tariff or raise prices [k]; raising prices makes its bicycles dearer than bloc-made rivals [app], so bloc sales volume and market share could fall [an].

choice between absorbing the tariff or raising prices

8% tariff / 55% of output / bloc-made rivals
analysis_max_2: squeeze on profit margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Vireo Bicycles should build the $1.8 million final-assembly facility inside the bloc, or stay in Country X and absorb the 8% tariff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the facility keeps tariff-free access to the bloc [k], saving $640,000 a year against the 8% tariff on $8 million of exports [app], so the $1.8 million cost could be recovered in under 3 years [an]. Staying in Country X avoids that investment and its risks [k]; absorbing $640,000 a year or raising prices may erode bloc demand, which is growing at 6% a year [app], damaging a market that takes 55% of output [an]. Overall, Vireo should build the facility, because the tariff saving and access to a market growing at 6% a year outweigh the $1.8 million cost [eval], provided the $1.8 million can be financed without straining cash flow [eval].

evaluation_max_2: weighs building the facility against absorbing the tariff; justified recommendation with figures

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Solano Solar Ltd is a multinational manufacturer of solar panels, operating for 10 years with 3 factories in the Aster Trade Bloc and 480 employees. Country A, a bloc member, offers zero tariff on imported silicon and a 25% tax incentive on factory setup costs; Country B, also in the bloc, offers wages of $900 a month against $1,400 in Country A but charges a 12% tariff on imported silicon.

Both countries give tariff-free access to the bloc's 210 million consumers. The new factory would serve customers across the bloc. The board must choose Country A or Country B for the new factory.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Thornbury Woollens Ltd is a yarn mill operating for 15 years with 180 employees in Country X, a member of the Aster Trade Bloc. Thornbury exports $5.2 million of yarn to 3 bloc countries and imports 175 of the 500 tonnes of wool it uses each year from outside the bloc at $2,400 per tonne.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Elmsgrove Apples is a family-owned apple grower operating for 12 years on 45 hectares in Country X, with 30 seasonal pickers and ten apple varieties in total. The government caps imported apples at 6,000 tonnes a year under an import quota; domestic apple prices rose from $1.40 to $1.85 per kg. Elmsgrove's revenue reached $1.1 million last season.

The agriculture ministry is reviewing whether to raise the quota to 9,000 tonnes to cut consumer prices. Supermarket chains want the higher limit, arguing consumers deserve lower prices and more choice. Elmsgrove argues this would flood the domestic market with cheaper apples and force it to lay off 10 pickers. The owner must decide whether to support the proposal or oppose it.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Salterns Furniture Ltd is a furniture manufacturer in Country X, operating for 8 years with 75 employees and annual revenue of $5.5 million. Its solid oak dining sets sell at about $800 each. The Meridian Trade Bloc has just admitted two new member countries, creating a combined tariff-free market of 160 million consumers for quality dining furniture. Salterns could export to the new member markets but would need $900,000 for distribution and to meet local safety standards.

The managing director projects first-year bloc sales of $2 million, rising to $3.5 million in year three. Alternatively, Salterns could expand its domestic sales team, which is cheaper, but the domestic market is growing at only 2% a year. The board must decide whether to invest in exporting or stay domestic.

Reason 2: First-year bloc sales are projected at $2 million, rising to $3.5 million in year three [k], outstripping domestic expansion [app].
